items.followUp: Explain how the shape of an enzyme’s active site relates to its substrate.

rubric.why: The model explains enzyme specificity through the matching shapes of the enzyme and substrate.
rubric.description: States that the active site has a specific shape that matches its substrate.
rubric.how: Require the active site, the substrate and a specific or matching shape.

rubric.why: In the model, substrate binding forms an enzyme-substrate complex; products are released and the enzyme remains unchanged.
rubric.description: Describes binding and product release, with the enzyme unchanged after the reaction.
rubric.how: Require the complex or binding, product release, and the unchanged enzyme.

modelAnswer: The enzyme’s active site has a specific shape that matches its substrate, just as a key fits a particular lock.
The substrate binds to the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex; products are released and the enzyme remains unchanged.

items.followUp: What is a coenzyme, and how does it help an enzyme?

rubric.why: A cofactor is distinguished from the protein part of an enzyme by being non-protein.
rubric.description: Defines a cofactor as a non-protein component.
rubric.how: Require that the component is described as non-protein.

rubric.why: A cofactor is required for or assists enzyme function.
rubric.description: States that the cofactor helps an enzyme function or is required for its activity.
rubric.how: Require a clear link between the cofactor and enzyme function or activity.

modelAnswer: A cofactor is a non-protein component required by some enzymes.
It helps the enzyme function or become active.

items.followUp: How is pulse rate related to the heartbeat?

rubric.why: A heartbeat is one cycle of the heart’s rhythmic activity.
rubric.description: Defines a heartbeat as the heart’s rhythmic cycle of contraction and relaxation.
rubric.how: Require the heart’s rhythmic action and both contraction and relaxation.

rubric.why: Pulse rate is the number of arterial pulses counted per minute.
rubric.description: Defines pulse rate as the number of pulses in the arteries per minute.
rubric.how: Require pulses counted per minute and identify their arterial location.

modelAnswer: A heartbeat is one rhythmic cycle of contraction and relaxation of the heart.
Pulse rate is the number of pulses in the arteries per minute, produced by the heartbeats.

items.followUp: Describe what happens to the diaphragm, ribs and air pressure during inhalation and exhalation.

rubric.why: Contraction and flattening of the diaphragm, together with the ribs moving up and out, bring about inhalation.
rubric.description: States the diaphragm and rib movements during inhalation.
rubric.how: Require the diaphragm to contract and flatten and the ribs to move up and out.

rubric.why: Chest expansion lowers lung pressure below atmospheric pressure, causing air to enter.
rubric.description: Connects increased thoracic volume and decreased pressure with air entering the lungs.
rubric.how: Require the pressure change and inward airflow, linked to expansion.

rubric.why: Relaxation of the diaphragm and the ribs moving down and in bring about exhalation.
rubric.description: States the diaphragm and rib movements during exhalation.
rubric.how: Require the diaphragm to relax and become dome-shaped and the ribs to move down and in.

rubric.why: A smaller chest cavity raises lung pressure and drives air out.
rubric.description: Connects decreased thoracic volume and increased pressure with air leaving the lungs.
rubric.how: Require the pressure change and outward airflow, linked to reduced volume.

modelAnswer: Inhalation (inspiration): the diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostal muscles raise the ribs up and out.
The thoracic cavity expands; lung pressure falls below atmospheric pressure, so air enters the lungs.
Exhalation (expiration): the diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped, and the ribs move down and in as the intercostal muscles relax.
The thoracic cavity becomes smaller; lung pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, so air is forced out.

items.followUp: Name the cell types in xylem and phloem, and state the function of each tissue.

rubric.why: Compound tissues consist of different kinds of cells working together.
rubric.description: Defines compound tissues as tissues made of different cell types that work together.
rubric.how: Require both multiple cell types and their cooperation in a function.

rubric.why: Vessels, tracheids, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres are the principal components of xylem.
rubric.description: Names the four main components of xylem.
rubric.how: Require all four components; accept either spelling of fibres.

rubric.why: Xylem transports water and mineral salts from roots towards leaves.
rubric.description: States that xylem carries water and minerals from the roots towards the leaves.
rubric.how: Require the materials transported and the direction or source and destination.

rubric.why: Sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres are the principal components of phloem.
rubric.description: Names the four main components of phloem.
rubric.how: Require all four components; accept either spelling of fibres.

rubric.why: Phloem transports food made in leaves to other parts of the plant.
rubric.description: States that phloem transports or translocates food from leaves to other parts of the plant.
rubric.how: Require food transport and identify leaves as its source or other plant parts as its destination.

modelAnswer: Compound tissues consist of different types of cells that work together to perform a common function.
Xylem is made up of vessels, tracheids, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.
Xylem carries water and mineral salts from the roots towards the leaves and also provides support.
Phloem is made up of sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres.
Phloem transports (translocates) food made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

items.followUp: Describe how bile helps in the digestion of fats and name one other important function of the liver.

rubric.why: The question asks whether the liver is a vital organ.
rubric.description: Identifies the liver as a vital or essential organ.
rubric.how: Require an explicit statement that the liver is vital or essential.

rubric.why: Bile is the liver’s main digestive secretion.
rubric.description: States that the liver produces or secretes bile.
rubric.how: Require the liver to be identified as the source of bile.

rubric.why: Bile salts emulsify large fat globules into smaller droplets.
rubric.description: Explains that bile emulsifies fats into small droplets.
rubric.how: Require emulsification or the breaking up of fat globules into smaller droplets.

rubric.why: Emulsification increases the surface area for lipase, and bile also helps neutralise acidic chyme.
rubric.description: Explains a digestive benefit of bile, such as aiding lipase action or neutralising acidic chyme.
rubric.how: Require one correct explanation of how bile assists digestion.

modelAnswer: The liver is a vital organ and the largest gland of the body; it performs essential functions, including processing nutrients and detoxifying harmful substances.
It produces bile, which is stored in the gall bladder and released into the small intestine.
Bile salts emulsify large fat globules into tiny droplets; bile is not an enzyme.
This increases the surface area for lipase to digest fats, and the alkaline bile also helps neutralise acidic chyme from the stomach.
